newsitem.title: PERU: Seasoned Peru rebel leads jungle fight.
newsitem.headline: Seasoned Peru rebel leads jungle fight.

text.p: Fighting for a revolution that never comes, Comrade Alejandro looks back at his secret life in Peru's jungle highlands and muses that he should write a book to tell his side of the bloody story.

But, numbed as he is by years of fighting, the memoirs of a senior Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebel -- a man who says killing is as easy as eating breakfast -- would not make for a light read.
"One tends to see our problems in a romantic light. The reality of the jungle is painful," he told Reuters as he trudged along a muddy trail on the eastern slopes of the Andes in the Junin region.
In Lima, 200 miles (320 km) to the west, about 20 of his jungle-trained comrades have been holed up with 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence for more than three months.

"It's not quite San Isidro, is it?" Alejandro asked, comparing the peasant shacks tucked into the hillsides with the scene at Latin America's longest hostage siege in a leafy, middle-class district of the capital.
"You can understand poverty by studying it, but here you feel it," said the former engineeering undergraduate, who used to belong to Peru's middle-class.
Alejandro identifies himself as a member of the MRTA's high command, fighting on behalf of Peru's forgotten poor.
President Alberto Fujimori labels him, like all rebels, a common criminal whose murders and extortion have stunted the country's growth.

In the early 1980s, just as the MRTA was taking root among jungle peasants -- thanks to its Robin Hood tactics of robbing the rich to give to the poor -- Alejandro left his Lima university for Peru's central jungle and a rebel's life of anonymity.
Now, as the MRTA's central jungle military leader, he burns anything he writes down. He set fire to his letters and mementoes long ago and the last photograph of him was taken in 1989.
Dressed in olive fatigues, a green peaked cap and rubber rainboots, the short, mid-30's rebel has a jutting jaw that seems always to wear an unnerving grin beneath his hollowed cheeks.
As he paused on a path high in the forest to contemplate the steamy jungle's beauty, cradling his polished AKM rifle, stillness, he answered questions.
His dark eyes assumed an empty stare as he said his nomadic life taught him to avoid falling in love. "I am only human, but I do not complicate my life with those things now."

Once, during an undercover operation in Lima, Alejandro found himself in front of his best friend from schooldays. Faced with a barrage of emotional questions about his "disappearance," he told his former friend there was some mistake and simply walked away.
While he may shun personal ties, the bonds with his comrades touch a nerve. Alejandro said he would dedicate his book to "the many comrades who have fallen along the way."

The MRTA's armed force, which experts say numbers no more than 200, was ruthlessly cut down from as many as 1,000 in the late 1980s. Alejandro remembers that military offensive as the "dark" stage but he prefers to talk about the camaraderie.
"What a memory I would need to tell all the jokes, stories and experiences ... all the experiences," he said.

He said he regrets not having had a camera last year when he watched a "special forces" MRTA squad blow up an army base, killing 30 men. "It was like a film," he recounted. "The building lifted up, hung in the air for a moment and then crashed down. Those soldiers died without even knowing they died."
That strike was "satisfying," he said.

But after more than a decade in the jungle, eating peasant handouts and sleeping outdoors, the Dec. 17 storming of the Japanese residence by a mainly teenage MRTA unit has the veteran rebel feeling good.
"Every expert was left stunned," he said. "In military terms, or with respect to its impact, it has been the best ever (guerrilla attack) in Latin America."
He said the headline-grabbing assault has also excited the MRTA's young jungle rebels who, joining up as young as 12, now hope to take part in such an operation.

A ceremonial parade may greet his arrival at training camp, but a relaxed Alejandro is happy to joke with the trainee rebels he calls his sons. "They have come to film you so all the girls in Lima can see you," he told the teenagers, who had turned from aggressive rebel chants to shy giggles in front of a camera.

The Lima hostage-taking has not only encouraged the MRTA's rank-and-file but "has resurrected the movement in the eyes of the public," Alejandro said. The MRTA, however, is still too weak to fulfil every member's dream of taking power, he said.

Fujimori came to power in 1990 and vigorously carried out much of his election promise to wipe out "terrorism" in Peru, virtually dismantling the MRTA and the larger, bloodier Shining Path by slamming rebel leaders in jail.
"Our main success is that we continue to exist," Alejandro said.
